newsitem.title: USA: Ratings mixed on muni disclosure effectiveness.
newsitem.headline: Ratings mixed on muni disclosure effectiveness.

text.p: Municipal bond issuers and buyers at a Florida conference had mixed reviews on the effectiveness of the new SEC rule requiring disclosure of information that could affect bond value.
Many of those who spoke at the Bond Buyer's Florida Public Finance Conference, which ends Friday, said they were still uncertain what exactly should be disclosed.
And while SEC rule 15-C212 does specify a dozen "material events" that could affect municipal credit, several issuers were hazy on exactly how the information should be offered, and for how long.
"I think if we could agree to a standardized set of disclosure forms it would benefit both the issuers and the marketplace," said Broward County Finance Director Phil Allen.
"I doubt that there is any investor in this room who would say, 'These meet my information needs,'" agreed Jim Marling, finance director for the city of Pensacola.

But Marling said municipalities could err in disclosing everything. He specifically cited a decision not to disclose a monthly drop in airport passenger revenues which turned out to be a temporary blip that was more than offset the next month.
"The moment you start doing that, you're going to spook the market," he said.
Marling also said that some investors who previously complained about a lack of information now seem uninterested when issuers offer it.

John Pomeroy, a portfolio manager for Franklin Advisers Inc, said some issuers who had been very forthcoming in the past had reduced their disclosure when the rule took effect, and now report only the minimum legally required.
"15-C212 at times can be self defeating," Pomeroy said.

"I'm not sure that a lot of bond counsel really get it yet. I have a lot of concern about bond counsel telling people not to disclose things, to disclose as little as possible," said William Oliver, director of municipal research at Alliance Capital Management.
Several panelists said swap agreements related to the bonds should be disclosed, as should any major change in revenues during the budget year.
"If you think there's something that could be a problem, it's probably a problem and you probably ought to disclose it," Oliver said.

Virgina Rutledge, chief financial officer for the Orlando Utilities Commission, advocated a golden rule approach: "If you communicate with the other guy that which you would want to be communicated if the roles are reversed, you're probably treating people fairly."
Oliver predicted that whatever the rule's shortcomings, it was more likely to be rewritten and fine-tuned than to be abolished.
"If this process doesn't work, it's not the last effort we're going to see," Oliver said.
